cards.statement: A map is a scaled, two-dimensional representation of part of the Earth's surface; its scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance.
cards.reasoning: Scale 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground.

cards.statement: Munnar, in Idukki district at about 1,500 m, is an example of a plateau (the high-range upland) in the Western Ghats of Kerala.
cards.reasoning: Kerala has highland, midland and lowland zones; Munnar is highland.

cards.statement: The nebular hypothesis (Kant and Laplace) says the Sun and planets formed from one rotating cloud of gas and dust; it is the most widely accepted model.
cards.reasoning: A spinning cloud flattens into a disc. This explains why all planets orbit in the same direction and nearly the same plane.
cards.source_ref: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)

cards.statement: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are terrestrial (rocky, dense) planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are Jovian (large, low-density) planets. The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
cards.reasoning: Near the hot young Sun only rock and metal could condense. Farther out, gas and ice could collect, making giant planets.

cards.statement: The Earth is about 4.55 billion years old, an age first fixed by Clair Patterson (1956) from lead isotopes in meteorites.
cards.reasoning: Earth's first rocks were destroyed by later melting and recycling. Meteorites formed at the same time and stayed unchanged, so they give the true age.

cards.statement: Circum-Pacific belt releases about 80% of earthquake energy (about 68% of earthquakes by number in some Indian texts); Alpine-Himalayan belt is second (about 15-21%); mid-ocean ridges third.
cards.reasoning: The Pacific is ringed by subduction zones, which store and release the most strain. Ridges give only small, shallow shocks.

cards.subtopic: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.statement: Rock strength increases with confining pressure and decreases as temperature rises.
cards.reasoning: Pressure presses cracks shut, so the rock is harder to break. Heat softens the rock so it flows more easily.

cards.statement: By the law of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers the lowest bed is the oldest and the topmost bed is the youngest.
cards.reasoning: Steno's law: you lay new layers on top of old ones.

cards.statement: The crystalline basement rocks of Kerala (charnockite, gneiss and khondalite) are Precambrian, mainly Archaean to Proterozoic in age.
cards.reasoning: They are the oldest rocks of the state; sedimentary rocks are only Tertiary and Quaternary.

cards.subtopic: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.statement: Stress is force per unit area (SI unit: pascal). Strain is the change in shape or volume that stress produces, and it has no units.
cards.reasoning: Stress is the cause, strain is the effect. Strain is a ratio (change in length / original length), so the units cancel.

cards.subtopic: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.statement: The strain ellipsoid is the shape a sphere takes after homogeneous strain. Its axes are X ≥ Y ≥ Z: longest, intermediate and shortest.
cards.reasoning: Think of squeezing a ball of clay: it becomes an egg or a disc. X is the stretch direction, Z is the squeeze direction.

cards.subtopic: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.statement: Pure shear is coaxial (non-rotational) strain. Simple shear is non-coaxial (rotational) strain.
cards.reasoning: Pure shear = squeezing a block flat; the strain axes do not turn. Simple shear = pushing the top of a pack of cards sideways; the strain axes rotate.

cards.subtopic: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.statement: Ionic radius is the main control on substitution: ions of similar size (within about 15%) and balanced charge can replace one another in a crystal lattice (Goldschmidt's rules).
cards.reasoning: Think of fitting a similar-sized brick into the same hole.

cards.statement: Coalification (peat to lignite to bituminous coal to anthracite) releases methane, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water as by-products while the coal becomes richer in carbon.
cards.reasoning: The coal loses its volatile parts and keeps the carbon.

cards.statement: Most of the methane in a coal seam is held by adsorption on the internal surfaces of coal micropores, not as free gas; lowering the pressure by pumping out water releases it.
cards.reasoning: Gas molecules stick on the organic surface like a film.

cards.statement: Gas hydrate is an ice-like water cage around gas molecules. Methane, ethane, CO2 and H2S form structure I; larger propane and isobutane form structure II.
cards.reasoning: Bigger guest molecules need bigger cages.

cards.statement: Kerala's best-known china clay deposit is at Kundara (Kollam district); the state holds about 23% of India's china clay resources (IBM, IMY 2022; inventory as on 1.4.2015).
cards.reasoning: The clay occurs in the Tertiary Warkalli beds and as residual clay over weathered gneiss. Thonnakkal near Thiruvananthapuram is another centre.

cards.statement: India has no working potash mine and imports its potash; potash salts (polyhalite, sylvite) are known in the buried evaporites of the Nagaur-Ganganagar basin, Rajasthan.
cards.reasoning: Potash salts form only in the last stage of sea water evaporation and dissolve easily, so they survive only deep underground. Status as known in 2025.

cards.statement: A sill is a sheet-like (tabular) concordant intrusion: it lies parallel to the bedding or foliation of the country rock.
cards.reasoning: Concordant means it follows the layers. Memory hook: a window sill lies flat, like the beds.

cards.statement: A dyke is a tabular discordant intrusion: it cuts across the bedding or foliation of the country rock.
cards.reasoning: Discordant means it cuts the layers. Dykes fill cracks, so they are usually steep. Dolerite is the commonest dyke rock.

cards.statement: A laccolith is a concordant intrusion with a flat floor and a domed roof, usually built by viscous acid (silica-rich) magma.
cards.reasoning: Thick, sticky magma cannot spread far sideways. It piles up and lifts the roof beds, like a mushroom cap.

cards.statement: By crystallinity, igneous rocks are holocrystalline (all crystals), holohyaline (all glass, like obsidian) or hypocrystalline (crystals plus glass).
cards.reasoning: Holo = whole, hyaline = glassy. Glass forms when lava cools too fast for crystals to grow.

cards.statement: Slow cooling at depth gives coarse (phaneritic) grains because few nuclei form and grow large; fast cooling of lava gives fine (aphanitic) grains or glass.
cards.reasoning: Nuclei are the tiny starting points of crystals. Slow cooling = few nuclei, big crystals. Fast cooling = many nuclei, tiny crystals.

cards.statement: Porphyritic texture has large crystals (phenocrysts) set in a finer groundmass, usually recording two stages of cooling; with a glassy groundmass it is called vitrophyric.
cards.reasoning: The big crystals grew slowly at depth. Then the magma rose and the rest cooled quickly around them.

cards.statement: Volcanic rock permeability varies: vesicular, jointed or rubbly-topped basalt can be a good aquifer, but dense massive lava (basalt or rhyolite) is nearly tight; unweathered igneous and metamorphic rocks are generally tight.
cards.reasoning: Permeability comes from vesicles, joints, rubbly flow tops and lava tubes, not from rock name.

cards.statement: The Indo-Gangetic alluvium is India's most productive aquifer system: thick sand-gravel beds, river, canal and rainfall recharge give very high yields and large groundwater resources.
cards.reasoning: Think thick, loose sand-gravel plus big rivers.

cards.statement: Evaporation absorbs about 590 calories per gram of water (latent heat of vaporisation near 15 C, about 2.47 MJ/kg) and continues until the air above is saturated.
cards.reasoning: This heat comes from the water and surroundings, which is why evaporation cools.

cards.subtopic: Types of wells and well construction
cards.statement: Bored wells are made with hand or rotary augers in soft ground; they are shallow, commonly up to about 30 m deep (limit varies by textbook).
cards.reasoning: Auger = a big screw that bores into soil.

cards.statement: In the Standard Penetration Test, the N value is the number of blows of a 63.5 kg hammer needed to drive the split-spoon sampler through the last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive.
cards.reasoning: N tells how dense or stiff a soil is. Engineering-geology item, outside the listed syllabus.

cards.statement: In neutron-capture (pulsed-neutron) logging, chlorine in saline water has a high thermal-neutron capture cross-section, so a high capture reading points to a saline water-bearing formation.
cards.reasoning: Chlorine absorbs slow neutrons strongly.
